title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding

paper.title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding
paper.abstract:
Abstract Discrete diffusion models have steadily improved in quality relative to autoregressive (AR) models. However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Discrete diffusion models have recently gained traction in language modeling ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2023 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , music synthesis ( Sun et al., 2022 ) , and biological sequence design ( Schiff et al., 2025 ) . Compared to autoregressive (AR) models, they offer faster generation ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) and improved controllability ( Schiff et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . However, they typically rely on architectures that preclude flexible-length generation ( Kim et al., 2025a ) and require full bidirectional context, which prevents key-value (KV) caching ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Nguyen-Tri et al., 2025 ) . Block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) partially mitigates these challenges by modeling sequences autoregressively over contiguous left-to-right blocks with discrete diffusion applied within each block. This yields a tighter likelihood bound, variable-length generation, and KV caching for previously decoded blocks. However, rigid left-to-right block structure restricts decoding flexibility for tasks requiring any-order generation such as infilling and arbitrary-position insertions ( Li et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2026 ) . Arriola et al. (2025a) also must delay KV cache updates until after a block is finished decoding because within-block denoising relies on bidirectional context ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Seo et al., 2025 ) . Finally, block diffusion limits parallel sampling since each block must be decoded before advancing ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Our key observation is that diffusion language models need not interpolate between autoregression and diffusion by varying a fixed block size; instead, they can interpolate by varying the order in which token sets are generated. Based on this, we introduce set diffusion, which defines an autoregressive probability distribution over flexible-position, flexible-length sets of discrete random variables. Set diffusion generalizes block diffusion: fixed left-to-right blocks arise when sets are constrained to contiguous fixed-size blocks, while arbitrary-position and variable-length sets enable flexible insertion, infilling, and sliding-window decoding. By interpolating between left-to-right and fully random orderings, set diffusion improves the tradeoff between sample quality, inference efficiency, and decoding flexibility while supporting KV cache updates after every generation step. Across mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation, set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion language models and substantially outperforms block diffusion on infilling. Figure 1 : Left: Set diffusion generates tokens in arbitrary-position, arbitrary-length sets, biasing toward left-to-right decoding and updating the KV cache after each step. Block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) is restricted to generate fixed-size sequential blocks and may only update the cache after each block completes. Right: Speed-accuracy tradeoffs on the GSM8K test (experimental details in Section L ). Our contributions are as follows: 1. We present set diffusion language models, which are autoregressive over flexible-length, flexible-position token sets, enabling variable-length generation and tunable generation orderings. 2. We introduce a set-causal diffusion architecture with KV cache updates after every inference step. 3. We show that set diffusion interpolates between AR and diffusion generation, enabling greater decoding flexibility and parallelism than block diffusion. 4. We demonstrate that set diffusion achieves state-of-the-art speed-quality tradeoffs among diffusion models across mathematical reasoning, infilling, summarization, and unconditional generation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Block Diffusion Language Modeling
sections.text: Block diffusion language models (BD3LM; Arriola et al. (2025a) ) interpolate between AR and order-agnostic diffusion by factorizing the likelihood over B B blocks of length S S . Adopting the shorthand from Arriola et al. (2025a) , we denote tokens in block index b ∈ [ 1 , B ] b\in[1,B] as 𝐱 b {\mathbf{x}}^{b} and preceding tokens as 𝐱 < b {\mathbf{x}}^{<b} . The likelihood factorizes as log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ∑ b = 1 B log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 b ∣ 𝐱 < b ) , \log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\log p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{b}\mid{\mathbf{x}}^{<b}), where each p θ ​ ( 𝐱 b ∣ 𝐱 < b ) p_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}^{b}\mid{\mathbf{x}}^{<b}) is modeled using diffusion. A block-causal transformer parameterizes the reverse process p θ ​ ( 𝐳 s b ∣ 𝐳 t b , 𝐱 < b ) p_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{b}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{b},{\mathbf{x}}^{<b}) , permitting KV caching for each block once decoded. However, rigid block-wise factorization limits both flexibility and speed: each block must be decoded before the next, restricting parallel sampling and arbitrary-position editing (e.g., infilling), and KV caches may only be updated once a block is completed.

sections.heading: 3 Set Diffusion
sections.text: We introduce set diffusion models, which factorize generation over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets. By varying the token-set partition and ordering distribution, set diffusion recovers autoregression, fully non-autoregressive diffusion ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Ou et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) , and block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) as special cases. We present a likelihood parameterization that supports variable-length sampling and a set-causal architecture that enables KV cache updates after every inference step.

sections.text: We train set diffusion models using maximum likelihood estimation by minimizing the NELBO in ( 3 ). Training is especially tractable for a fixed ordering distribution π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) that is independent of the data and model parameters. In this setting, we may first sample σ ∼ π \sigma\sim\pi and then approximate ℒ SD ​ ( 𝐱 , θ ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{SD}}({\mathbf{x}};\theta) using Monte Carlo with a single ordering ∑ n = 1 N ℒ ⁡ ( 𝐱 σ n , 𝐱 < σ n , θ ) \sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{x}}^{\sigma_{n}},{\mathbf{x}}^{<\sigma_{n}};\theta) . Learned orderings are also compatible with set diffusion, but optimizing them requires propagating gradients through discrete sampling ( Wang et al., 2025c ) ; we leave this for future work.

sections.heading: 4 Interpolating Between Token Orderings
sections.text: We now describe a structured family of ordering distributions π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) that interpolates between order-agnostic diffusion and autoregression by changing the order in which token positions are revealed. We specialize to fixed, data- and parameter-independent ordering distributions induced by position-dependent reveal-time schedules. This interpolation controls the speed–quality tradeoff in set diffusion: order-agnostic generation enables larger, more flexible token sets for parallel decoding, while stronger left-to-right bias tightens the NELBO and improves sample quality. Block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) instantiates this tradeoff by varying a block size, but its fixed contiguous blocks restrict arbitrary-position insertion. Instead, we parameterize π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) through position-dependent reveal-time distributions: each token position is assigned a random reveal time, and sorting the sampled reveal times induces a generation order. The resulting position-offset schedules provide a simple mechanism for controlling left-to-right bias while retaining flexible-position decoding.

sections.heading: 5 Sliding-Window Set Diffusion Language Models (SW-SetDLMs)
sections.text: We introduce Sliding-Window Set Diffusion Language Models (SW-SetDLMs), a practical instantiation of set diffusion with a position-offset ordering distribution π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) , a factorized token-set likelihood, and an order-causal transformer architecture. These choices enable variable-length sliding-window decoding, KV cache updates after each inference step, and low-variance training. Unlike block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) , SW-SetDLMs decode flexible-position, flexible-length sets while preserving a left-to-right bias for high-quality generation.

sections.heading: Optimization
sections.text: We optimize SW-SetDLMs with set diffusion training specialized to singleton token sets (Section 3.3 ). For each sampled ordering, a single causal forward pass computes all L L conditional terms in Eq. 9 . Unlike prior masked diffusion objectives, which compute gradients only from masked tokens ( Arriola et al., 2025a ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , SW-SetDLM uses every token position, reducing gradient variance. The same objective supports one-pass full-sequence likelihood computation, useful for applications including efficient policy-gradient estimation in reinforcement learning ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Sahoo et al., 2025b ) .

sections.heading: Comparison to MDLMs
sections.text: Set diffusion builds on denoising discrete diffusion ( Austin et al., 2021 ) and recent MDLMs focusing on masking noise ( Lou et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , with two key improvements: (1) prior diffusion language models use order-agnostic ordering schedules, whereas we employ position-dependent ordering schedules that tighten the ELBO; (2) our causal diffusion architecture enables KV caching and variable-length generation, which prior approaches do not support. Although Kim et al. (2025b) ; Seo et al. (2025) ; Shu et al. (2026) explore non-uniform generation orders, they rely on heuristic ordering rather than our principled per-token noise parameterization, and their bidirectional transformer precludes flexible-length generation and KV caching. Esoteric Language Models ( Sahoo et al., 2025b ) also interpolate between diffusion and AR, but do so using an order-agnostic diffusion stage before left-to-right AR completion, rather than defining a diffusion process with a left-to-right generation bias. While they also use a causal architecture for KV caching, their training objective applies supervision only at randomly masked positions, resulting in sparser training signals than our objective, and they do not explore variable-length generation. WeDLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) adopts a causal transformer architecture for KV caching but does not support variable-length generation or tunable interpolation between diffusion and AR.

sections.heading: Comparison to Block Diffusion
sections.text: Block diffusion models ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) (also known as semi-autoregressive models ( Han et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2023 ) ) unmask tokens in strict left-to-right blocks, which sacrifices infilling flexibility and restricts parallelism, as each block must be fully decoded before advancing. In contrast, we support decoding in sliding-window sets. While Arriola et al. (2025a) update KV caches once a block is fully decoded, we update the KV cache after every inference step for greater efficiency.

sections.heading: Comparison to FlexMDM
sections.text: FlexMDM ( Kim et al., 2025a ) also uses any-order autoregression for flexible-length diffusion sampling. However, it introduces separate schedules for masked token insertion and unmasking, requires a separate insertion network to predict inserted tokens at each step, and uses a bidirectional transformer to parameterize token likelihoods, precluding KV caching. In contrast, set diffusion explicitly models generation order, supports flexible-length generation without an insertion network while adhering to a user-specified inference budget, and enables KV caching.

sections.heading: Comparison to Any-Order Autoregressive Models
sections.text: Our objective is related to the AO-ARM ( Uria et al., 2014 ) , whose objective is equivalent to fully non-AR diffusion ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Ou et al., 2024 ; Uria et al., 2014 ; Shih et al., 2022 ) . Unlike prior AO-ARMs which optimize over uniform orders and sample a single trajectory step during training ( Uria et al., 2014 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Ou et al., 2024 ) , SW-SetDLMs use non-uniform orders and efficiently predict all token likelihoods simultaneously. While Shih et al. (2022) allow non-uniform π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) , their method cannot flexibly interpolate ordering distributions and uses a bidirectional transformer, preventing KV caching and variable-length inference. Methods that learn orderings via variational inference ( Wang et al., 2025c ) or confidence-based unmasking policies ( Kim et al., 2026 ) require complex optimization to discover effective orderings, whereas we impose a structured prior over π ⁡ ( σ ) \pi(\sigma) motivated by the success of block-wise generation ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Although the gap between set diffusion and autoregression has narrowed, there is still a tradeoff between accuracy and parallelization in tuning the position-offset ordering schedules. The ideal schedule can be hand-tuned based on user preferences and/or parallelization capabilities of the inference hardware, or learned throughout training ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) .

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This work introduces set diffusion, a framework for interpolating between AR and diffusion decoding by tuning generation orders rather than fixed block structure. Set diffusion supports flexible-length generation and KV caching with a causal diffusion architecture, achieving state-of-the-art speed-quality tradeoffs across benchmarks.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

This quantity corresponds to the expected number of tokens eligible for prediction at a given ordering time, averaged over the generation trajectory. A token is “eligible” at ordering time τ \tau if it has not yet been selected for generation and τ \tau lies in its active generation interval. For a reveal-time variable R ℓ R^{\ell} , the probability that the ℓ \ell -th token has not yet been selected is the survival probability Pr ⁡ ( R ℓ > τ ) = 1 − α τ ℓ \Pr(R^{\ell}>\tau)=1-\alpha_{\tau}^{\ell} . sections.heading: Appendix L Experimental Details
sections.text: For GSM8K and CNN/DailyMail, we use AdamW with weight decay 1 ​ e − 5 1e^{-5} and ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.98 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.98) . For OWT and LM1B, we use AdamW with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) and no weight decay, following Sahoo et al. (2024) ; Arriola et al. (2025a) . We apply gradient clipping with a maximum norm of 1.0 1.0 . We maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of model parameters with decay rate 0.9999, and use the EMA model for evaluation. For decoding, we use confidence-based greedy decoding ( Nie et al., 2024 ) . For parallel sampling, we use confidence-aware parallel decoding with tuned confidence thresholds ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . All reported decoding throughput measurements use inference batch size 1 on a single H100 80GB GPU. For unconditional generation using models trained on OWT and LM1B, throughput is instead measured on four RTX A6000 48GB GPUs.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: For GSM8K, we distill a student model initialized from Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base to support parallel diffusion decoding, following the adaptation approach of Arriola et al. (2025b) . Distillation mitigates catastrophic forgetting by training the student on responses generated by a stronger teacher model, aligning the adaptation objective with the teacher’s output distribution. Concretely, we construct the training set by prompting Qwen/Qwen3-32B-Base with each GSM8K training question and using the resulting responses as targets. We construct the validation set analogously by prompting Qwen/Qwen3-32B-Base with the GSM8K validation questions and using the resulting responses as validation targets. The prompts are drawn from the main configuration of the GSM8K dataset ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , downloaded from https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k . We preprocess each input by prepending the instruction “ Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within $\boxed{}$. ”. We preprocess each target by prepending “ Answer: ” and formatting the final answer as “ $\boxed{}$. ”. Inputs and targets are truncated to a maximum combined length of 1024 tokens.

sections.heading: Tokenization and Hyperparameters
sections.text: We used the Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base tokenizer. We use all the layers of the pretrained Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base model, which has a hidden size of 2048 and intermediate hidden size of 6144. We train with batch size 1. The learning rate is linearly warmed up for 100 steps to a maximum of 1 e − 5 \text{e}^{-5} and decayed using a cosine schedule to half the peak value. Models are trained for up to 75k steps with early stopping based on the validation loss to select the model with the best validation perplexity.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Models generate responses with a maximum length of 1024 tokens. Generation is deterministic and uses the same Set Diffusion decoding procedure as above. We stop generations using a boxed-answer regular-expression criterion, with an additional repeating-token guard; runs using the chat-template format additionally stop on the <|im_end|> token. Inference is performed using the lm-eval harness library with the ‘flexible match’ criterion, and the same preprocessing is applied to question texts. Solutions are reverted to their original ### <Answer> format. In Figure 1 , SW-SetDLM is trained with a maximum decoding window of 8 tokens, while block diffusion uses a block size of 4. At evaluation, both methods use a decoding block size of 4; SW-SetDLM supports sliding-window prediction and KV cache updates after every inference step, whereas block diffusion does not. We report zero-shot pass@1 accuracy and inference speed on an H100 80GB GPU over 200 samples, after a 50-sample warmup. For parallel decoding, we tune the confidence threshold over the set { 0.6 , 0.65 , 0.7 , … , 0.95 , 0.99 , 1.0 } \{0.6,0.65,0.7,\dots,0.95,0.99,1.0\} . For MDLM on GSM8K, we use a confidence threshold of 0.9, which we found to yield slightly better accuracy at higher throughput.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: For this task, we use the CNN/DailyMail dataset version 3.0 ( Hermann et al., 2015 ; See et al., 2017 ) downloaded from https://huggingface.co/datasets/abisee/cnn_dailymail . The samples are preprocessed by adding a prefix to summaries: “ Summary: ”. Inputs are truncated to a maximum length of 512 tokens and targets are truncated to a maximum length of 180 tokens, following the experimental setup of ( Lin et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023b ) .

sections.heading: Tokenization and Hyperparameters
sections.text: We use the Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base tokenizer. All models had a hidden size of 256, an intermediate hidden size of 768, and 28 transformer layers, corresponding to 80M parameters. We train with batch size 128. The learning rate is linearly warmed up for 1000 steps to a maximum of 3 e − 4 \text{e}^{-4} . Models are trained for up to 500k steps with early stopping to select the model with the best validation perplexity.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Models generate up to 180 additional tokens. ROUGE scores ( Lin, 2004 ) are computed using the evaluate library from HuggingFace. For all CNN/DailyMail models, we apply a repetition penalty of 1.2 1.2 , require at least 50 50 generated tokens, and use an exponential length penalty starting at 80 80 tokens with decay factor 1.1 1.1 . Decoding also uses an EOS/stop-string stopping criterion. Finally, for MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , we decode semi-autoregressively using a block size of 32.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: We train on OpenWebText (OWT; Gokaslan et al. (2019) ) dataset and the One Billion Word dataset (LM1B; Chelba et al. (2014) ). For OWT, we reserve the last 100K documents as a validation set. Following Arriola et al. (2025a) , we concatenate documents and wrap them to the model context length without padding or truncation, and do not insert [BOS] or [EOS] tokens at the beginning and end of the context to enable arbitrary-length generation. We use a context length of 1024 for OWT and 128 for LM1B.

sections.heading: Tokenization and Hyperparameters
sections.text: For OWT, we use the gpt2 tokenizer ( Radford et al., 2019 ) ; for LM1B, we use the bert-base-uncased tokenizer ( Devlin et al., 2018 ) . All models have 110M total parameters (excluding token embeddings). For models trained on OWT, we use a batch size of 512 and 300K total gradient updates. For models trained on LM1B, we use a batch size of 512 and 1M total gradient updates. The learning rate was linearly warmed up for 2500 steps to a peak of 3 ​ e − 4 3e^{-4} and held constant thereafter.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: For likelihood evaluation, we use a single-sample Monte Carlo estimator over latent variables t , 𝐳 t , σ t,{\mathbf{z}}_{t},\sigma . For unconditional generation, we sample 1K sequences from models trained on OWT and report MAUVE scores ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) against 1K samples from the OWT validation split. To reduce sensitivity to the particular validation subset, we fix each model’s 1K generated samples and compute MAUVE against five fixed random subsets of 1K OWT validation examples, reporting the mean across subsets. We also report average sentence entropy for diversity. For categorical decoding, we sample directly from the model’s predicted token distribution using multinomial sampling. Decoding throughput ( Tput ) is measured in tokens/sec on four RTX A6000 48GB GPUs. We report mean ± \pm standard deviation over 200 post-warmup samples with maximum length L ≤ 1024 L\leq 1024 , gathered across ranks after 50 warmup examples per rank, using each model’s configured sampling steps. For MAUVE, we use nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 p=0.95 and repetition penalty 1.05 1.05 for SetDLM and BD3LM, and p = 0.90 p=0.90 with no repetition penalty for AR. Generation stops after at least 128 tokens when the end-of-text confidence exceeds the stopping threshold for 4 consecutive windows of 128 tokens, or otherwise at L = 1024 L=1024 tokens.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: We perform infilling evaluation using models trained on OWT, following ( Guo and Ermon, 2025 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) . For this task, we follow Guo and Ermon (2025) and test on 1871 short stories from the ROCStories dataset ( Mostafazadeh et al., 2016 ) downloaded from Shen et al. (2023) . Each story contains five sentences.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: For each story, we mask either the middle sentence or the middle three sentences and have the model predict the missing span. ROUGE scores ( Lin, 2004 ) are computed using the evaluate library from HuggingFace. We use a repetition-penalty logits processor during generation, with factor 1.2. We record throughput on a single H100 80GB GPU.

However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. We provide the code 1 1 1 Code: https://github.com/kuleshov-group/setdlms , along with the model weights and blog post on the project page: https://m-arriola.com/setdlms/ Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML 1 Introduction Discrete diffusion models have recently gained traction in language modeling ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2023 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , music synthesis ( Sun et al., 2022 ) , and biological sequence design ( Schiff et al., 2025 ) . Compared to autoregressive (AR) models, they offer faster generation ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) and improved controllability ( Schiff et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . However, they typically rely on architectures that preclude flexible-length generation ( Kim et al., 2025a ) and require full bidirectional context, which prevents key-value (KV) caching ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Nguyen-Tri et al., 2025 ) . Block diffusion ( Arriola et al., 2025a ) partially mitigates these challenges by modeling sequences autoregressively over contiguous left-to-right blocks with discrete diffusion applied within each block. This yields a tighter likelihood bound, variable-length generation, and KV caching for previously decoded blocks. However, rigid left-to-right block structure restricts decoding flexibility for tasks requiring any-order generation such as infilling and arbitrary-position insertions ( Li et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2026 ) . Arriola et al. (2025a) also must delay KV cache updates until after a block is finished decoding because within-block denoising relies on bidirectional context ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Seo et al., 2025 ) . Finally, block diffusion limits parallel sampling since each block must be decoded before advancing ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Our key observation is that diffusion language models need not interpolate between autoregression and diffusion by varying a fixed block size; instead, they can interpolate by varying the order in which token sets are generated. Based on this, we introduce set diffusion, which defines an autoregressive probability distribution over flexible-position, flexible-length sets of discrete random variables. Set diffusion generalizes block diffusion: fixed left-to-right blocks arise when sets are constrained to contiguous fixed-size blocks, while arbitrary-position and variable-length sets enable flexible insertion, infilling, and sliding-window decoding. By interpolating between left-to-right and fully random orderings, set diffusion improves the tradeoff between sample quality, inference efficiency, and decoding flexibility while supporting KV cache updates after every generation step. Across mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation, set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion language models and substantially outperforms block diffusion on infilling. We specialize to fixed, data- and parameter-independent ordering distributions induced by position-dependent reveal-time schedules.
